title: Agentic AI, ESP32 Hacks, and Kernel Updates
intro: This week the AI‑agent playbook kept expanding while makers turned ESP32 chips into browsers and radios. Meanwhile, the Linux kernel got a security polish and a deprecation notice.

themes.headline: Agentic AI Gets More Tools
themes.body: **Lead‑in:** Researchers rolled out a suite of frameworks to audit, steer, and accelerate LLM‑driven agents. X‑RIC adds a telecom‑grade controller, BLADE audits failures, and ChunkAct bundles actions into single calls. SEAR tests skill transfer across simulation and reality, while CIPR and Claim Cards improve robustness and interpretability. Together they signal a push toward reliable, self‑correcting AI agents.

themes.headline: ESP32 Powers New Hacks
themes.body: **Lead‑in:** The ESP32 chip kept stealing the spotlight, from an in‑browser emulator (Esp32sim) to SDR experiments and even controlling an iPhone via an AI agent. Hackers also repurposed its RF front‑end for DVB‑S2 video and revived dead Onkyo receivers with open firmware. The trend shows low‑cost hardware becoming a sandbox for both software and signal‑processing creativity.

themes.headline: Kernel & Security Tightening
themes.body: **Lead‑in:** Linux’s 7.3‑rc7 prepatch arrived, deprecating ext4’s data=journal mode with removal slated for 2028. Security bulletins from LWN highlighted dozens of package patches across major distributions, underscoring the ongoing race to harden the stack. These updates remind engineers that the foundation must stay as fresh as the latest AI tricks.

themes.headline: Formal Methods & Benchmarks Rise
themes.body: **Lead‑in:** New theory and tooling aim to make AI workflows provably correct and data processing faster. FAOPs defines normal forms for agent pipelines, TraHist improves trajectory cardinality estimates, and JetStream auto‑generates verified query accelerators. A post‑quantum KEM benchmark measures overhead under 500 concurrent workers, highlighting performance concerns for future cryptography.
